title: The Invisible
full_review:
Unlike the original Swedish film on which this is based, "The Invisible" (Buena Vista) eschews the word "soul" in describing the ghostlike teen who wanders through his Pacific Northwest town, hoping to find justice for the beating that's left him near death, removing the spiritual dimension to what here is merely a violent story.

Nicholas Powell (Justin Chatwin) is a poetic high school senior setting his sights on a London writing program, against the wishes of his suffocatingly possessive, widowed mother (Marcia Gay Harden).

On the night after graduation when he had planned to sneak off, she guilt-trips him into not going. That puts Nick on a collision course with local tough girl Annie Newton (Margarita Levieva), who menaces Nick's friend, Pete (Chris Marquette), believing Pete informed on her about a burglary she had committed, whereas the squealer was actually her parolee boyfriend (Alex O'Loughlin). Figuring Nick's safely on a plane, Pete "confesses" under torture that Nick did it.

Annie and her two goons thereupon brutally attack Nick, then dump him down a manhole. The next day, Nick surprisingly seems none the worse for wear, and only a little foggy as he heads off to school. He appears, at first, to be able to interact with the world, but soon realizes no one can see him.

Nick spends most of the movie helplessly yelling in people's ears and generally mopes like a kid who just got turned down for a prom date. From there, the movie meanders through a police investigation and gunpoint double-crosses. Despite one heartbreaking scene with Nick's devastated mother, the movie only makes half-hearted points about teenagers' real selves being" invisible" to grown-ups.

Since the same screenwriter, Mick Davis, penned both the deeply emotional original and this inept remake, the blame must fall on comic-book screenwriter David S. Goyer, here directing his third film. Unconvincing plot points, inconsistent internal logic, a somnambulistic leading man and a preposterous, muddled climax inspire unintended laughter.

The film contains a few instances of crude and crass language, a mild scene of clothed groping, an implied night of premarital sex, brief shower-related female nudity, and much violence, including beatings and a scene of gunfire, though handled with relative discretion. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
